utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, the technical booth, the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, court reporters, the legal assistants, Ms. Niemann and Ms. Hollis; good morning, Defence counsel. I see we are complete. Good morning to the accused. We are going to resume today, with the normal composition of the Chamber, to continue our case. Mr. Niemann, I think we have a witness. I think it's your turn, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. We call Zuhra Hrnic as the witness this morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Hrnic. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration which the usher is going to give you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Are you comfortable, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So-so. So-so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, I'm sure you will have the strength to answer questions which Mr. Niemann is going to put to you. Mr. Niemann, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ms. Hrnic, were you born in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of March, 1935, in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that you worked there as a seamstress until 1990 when you retired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: My religion is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, on the 20th of June, 1992, I understand you were having coffee in the morning with your neighbour when you were arrested; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people that arrested you, who were they?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know them. Two young men in Serb uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think firstly they took you to Keraterm and you were there for a little while, and then they took you to the SUP in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think several hours later you were then taken with a group of seven other people to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ms. Hrnic, what happened when you arrived at the Omarska camp? Can you tell the Court that?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: What happened was that we were lined up next to the wall. We had to raise our arms and spread our legs for them to search us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was it that searched you?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The guards, most probably. They were guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These were the guards at the Omarska camp, were they?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you'd been searched, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Then me and a lady who was brought with me were taken to the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "the restaurant," what part of the camp is that? Can you give us some idea of the location of that?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The restaurant of the iron ore mine, where the camp was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is on the ground floor, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, how long did you stay in the restaurant on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Until the evening, between 7.00 and half past seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At about half past seven, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: At that time we went upstairs to these two sleeping rooms where the women slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to just go to the sleeping rooms or was permission needed to be had for you to go to a particular room; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Not permission, but it was -- our sort of room leader asked that the two of us be accommodated in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of your room leader?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Her name was Jadranka Cigelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who she asked so that you could go to that room?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Apparently someone called Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: She told you that, did she?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I don't think you were present when she actually asked for you to stay in that room.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, for the time that you were in the Omarska camp, apart from those two rooms that you have described, the kitchen or, I should say, the restaurant and the upstairs sleeping room, did you stay in any other part of the Omarska camp for the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From the place where you stayed in the Omarska camp, namely the restaurant and upstairs, could you have a view out of the restaurant to see what was happening around the camp at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how was it that you could see? What enabled you to be able to see out?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: When I wasn't washing up the dishes, we had to sit at a table next to very large windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And those windows look out over the camp, did they?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, they looked out at the hangar and the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And could you see people on the pista at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who were these people that you could see?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They were the inmates of the camp, men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I know that you could see them from day-to-day, but what were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: More often than not, they were lying face down on their stomach and during that period of 8 to 10 hours, they would sometimes be sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were they forced to lie down or were they just doing this apparently because they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They were probably forced to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were there guards overlooking these men that were on the pista?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what about in the building that you were located in where the restaurant was, did you see inmates in that building as well?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: From the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, or from the restaurant or from any of the part of the building that you were in. Could you see inmates inside your building?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Inmates inside the building we couldn't see except when they came for meals and, of course, not counting those we could see on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, from time to time, did you observe people being taken in or brought into this building that you were in?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They would come to eat into the building where I was, where I stayed from 7.00 in the morning until 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what duties were you forced to -- I'll withdraw that, Your Honour. What duties did you perform when you were there in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: We split up in two groups so one day I would do the washing up, and the next day I would just sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you ever have occasion to serve food to the prisoners or was that handled by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I did not. Not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to observe the food that was being served to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Of course, because I ate the same food too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what sort of food was it, can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I can. It was worthless. We would get a quarter of a loaf of bread daily, but most frequently it would be only an eighth of a loaf of moldy bread. Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Apart from bread, one day we would get beans which was more often than not sour. The next day would be soup, cabbage soup with only one leaf inside. The third day, a bit of rice. The food was really quite terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how many meals a day did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Only one meal in 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the one meal that you had in 24 hours, at what time of the day did they normally have that?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The meal lasted from 9.00 until 4.00 or 5.00. It also depended when the food arrived. Sometimes it came earlier, sometimes later, but as soon as it arrived, the distribution would start.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when the prisoners come to have their meal, were they restricted in terms of time in which to eat?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, three minutes. They had three minutes to come from the place where they were to eat and to go back to their place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, what happened if the men didn't finish their meal in three minutes?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you have any relatives in the camp at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't understand why they had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you tell His Honour why they had to do it, why they had to eat in three minutes? Could you answer that?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They were forced to finish their meal, otherwise they would get beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who would beat them?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The guards. The guards who were there in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in terms of the men moving through to get their meal, did all that have to take place in the three minutes, the collection of food and eating it as well?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Everything, everything. To take their plates, to eat it, and to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any relatives at all in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had two nephews, the sons of my two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you tell their honours approximately how old these two nephews were of yours at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: My younger brother's son was born in 1964 and the older one, believe me, I don't know exactly, but he was about 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's all I wanted you to tell us, a rough idea of their age. Now, did you have a chance to see them during the time that you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When they would come to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what could you see of them, could you describe their appearance when they came into the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I can't describe only my two nephews, all the inmates looked awful. They were unrecognisable. They had lost weight. They were skinny. They had -- didn't have a haircut. They hadn't shaved. They were dirty. What else could I say? And perhaps sometimes they were wet with urine, and I apologise for having to say it, but they were dirty as a result of dysentery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever have occasion to speak to them when they came in or was that prevented?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, on a number of occasions, I would save my eighth of a loaf and give it to one nephew the next day, and then the next day I would save again my piece of bread and give it to the other nephew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember a part of the building that you were in called the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately where that was in relation to the kitchen, or the restaurant, I should say?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the restaurant, and the way we entered the restaurant, the "glass house" would be on our right, and there was a wooden bar that we had to pass by to take our meals. The "glass house" was here and we went for our food here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any prisoners kept in the "glass house" that you could see while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you give me a very approximate idea of how many prisoners were in this area known as the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: In my estimate which may not be correct, but between 30 and 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people that were kept in the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I knew -- just a moment, please. I knew Reuf Travancic; he was an inspector in SUP, an investigator. Then I knew also Kusuran, a doctor. I knew another man, but just now -- and I'm so sorry -- I cannot recollect the surname, but I know that family very well because they are all from Prijedor. Yes, I've remembered. Suljanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about a Dr. Begic? Did you know a Dr. Begic?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I met Dr. Begic in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned, I think, a person by the name of Reuf Travancic.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anything happen to him that you were able to observe at the time that you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Everyone could see the injuries on his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In what way was his body injured? Can you give us a little bit more of a description?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: That man was black and blue -- I don't know how else I could describe it -- as a result of blows. He was almost unconscious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had he been beaten in the camp or outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: He came beaten up. Where he was beaten, I don't know, but most probably upstairs when he went for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone else in the "glass house," or anywhere else in the camp, that had been beaten in a similar way in the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Where they beat them, I don't know, but I saw men who had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned upstairs. You used to sleep upstairs; that's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who else used to occupy the area upstairs?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: On the first floor were the two rooms where the women slept; I assume it was in two rooms. Whether there was another room for interrogation, I don't know. But the room I slept in was used for the interrogators to interrogate the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know that your room was used by the interrogators to interrogate the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I know because we could never go there before 7.00 or half past seven, until they finished their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever have to clean up the rooms that you slept in?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Every evening before we went to sleep, we women would take turns to clean the room so that the other women could come into a clean room and go to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you find in the times that you had to clean up the room, the interrogation room where you slept? What did you find?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we would come across -- whether it was water or urine, I don't know, blood, chairs thrown around, things like that. That is what I personally saw. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see any implements or things that may have been used during the course of the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did anyone else, apart from the interrogators and you women that slept in this interrogation room, did anyone else stay upstairs?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, in the two rooms there, that's where we were. Across the corridor from us were the managers, administrators, the managers of the camp and those who were superior to the shifts that came on duty. I don't know how to explain that. They were actually the shift leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you say "managers," did you know any of these managers, the names of any of these managers?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: By name, I only knew Miro Kvocka by name, that is, before I came to the camp. During my stay in the camp, I got to know Zeljko Meakic. He was one of the first heads. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Then when Miroslav Kvocka left from that duty, Drago Prcac arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what position Miroslav Kvocka held when he was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the conclusions we made and according to their conduct and behaviour, it was Zeljko Meakic and Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you know Miroslav Kvocka before you went into the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't actually know him personally but I knew him by name. I knew his name and surname through a colleague at work, who worked with me in the same firm I worked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about Zeljko Meakic? Did you know him at all?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the commanders of the shift. Did you know any of these shift commanders or come to know them when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I came to know them while I was in the camp; otherwise, I didn't know any of them or hear about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of any of them that you came to know when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I got to know somebody nicknamed Krle, another nicknamed Krkan, and Ckalja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the women that were with you in the interrogation rooms, that slept with you in the interrogation rooms, are you able to give us the names of any of those women?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I forget one name, you'll forgive me, but I'll try. Can I go ahead and name them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Please do.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The first woman was Sena Delkic. The second was Munevera Mesic. The third woman was Advija Mahmuljic. Then there was Jadranka Kvocka -- no, Jadranka Cigelj was her name. Then there was Zlata Cikota, and there was Hasiba, known as Biba, Harambasic. There was Tidza; I'll probably remember her surname later on. Then there was Ms. Sada Hadzalic, and Sadeta Medunjanin. Then there was Sadija Avdic. There was a woman called Azra whose surname I don't know. Then there was Suada Ramic. There was Zumra or Zumreta Mehmedovic or Mehmedagic, I'm not quite sure of her surname. And then there was a woman called Valida, I don't know her surname either. There was Jovanka Divis, she left after 10 or 15 days in the camp, she left afterwards because she was a Serb but she was married to a Croat. And for the moment, I can't think of any more names but there was 17 of us women in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you tell Their honours, how it is you have that memory of the women that were in the room and be able to remember their names?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, you see, I have a fairly good memory, but spending a month and a half in the camp, I think I was able to remember the names of those women very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see a man in the camp, a prisoner by the name of Ibro Crnkic?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Crnkic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And had you known him or known of him before he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I had heard of him. He was a professor of mathematics. He taught mathematics and was a well-known figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to see him one day in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, two or three times at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did any of those two or three times, did he appear to be beaten or injured in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it was on that day or one day later, I heard his screams from the beatings, and I saw him being taken down from the floor above from being interrogated. And believe me when I say that I can still hear his cries when I'm sleeping at night. I still hear those screams and his prayers -- that is to say his entreaties to let him go. He said he was not guilty of anything. And to this, they would respond with blows. I didn't see that, but I heard the cursing. They swore and cursed his balija mother and they said that he was no brother of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you see his injuries after this beating?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them but you could notice that something was wrong with his arm, his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As best you can, can you describe to Their Honours what you saw about his hand and his arm?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw that it wasn't hanging in the right way, and he managed to show one of us inmates but I didn't see that actually, but he showed us his collar bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And from what you saw and from what you were told, do you understand that it must have been broken?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember a part of the camp that people would refer to as the "red house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I do remember, yes. I remember the "red house," but up until then, I didn't know about the "red house". I didn't notice it until one day. I don't remember the exact date, but they took the people off towards that house, towards the "red house" along the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you know any of the people that were taken off towards the "red house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The only person that I was able to see on the very corner of the hangar was Dr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when he was being taken to the "red house," was he being escorted there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't need to ask me about escorts, no -- none of the camp inmates went anywhere without an escort. So he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you know Dr. Begic before you went into the Omarska camp or know of him?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, I have already told you that I got to know Begic in Omarska itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. And after he went to the "red house," did you ever see him again in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, never again, and I don't know what happened to him. But unfortunately, and I do apologise if I may say this, he wasn't the only man led off towards the "red house".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know any of the others or see any of the others that were taken? I think you said you saw him. Is he the only one that you said you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, no, I only saw Begic, me, personally, that is. As for the other people who were taken away, according to those people who escorted them, I do know that, but I don't think it's up to me to say because I didn't actually see it happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's fine, that's fine. Did you know a place in the camp that was referred to as the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was this a building that you could see from your position in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Easily. I didn't have any trouble. It's just as if I was looking straight ahead of me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And could you see, from time to time, the happenings and events that were going on in and around the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Around the "white house," yes, but not actually in the "white house" itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell us what you saw from time to time.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw people, and in front of the "white house," for example, I saw them being lined up to wash them down with a hose. That was twice during my stay in Omarska. Then I saw daily up above the "white house," there was a wire fence where the inmates of the camp were taken out or brought there, and they were lined up along that wire fence. I assumed that these were dead detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And these people you saw lined up, they were laid down, were they, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I take it they appeared dead because they didn't move and were dragged to that place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who took these apparently dead people to this place?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Nobody took them, they were carried there, and usually it was the camp inmates who would perform these tasks. They weren't always the same ones, they would change depending on who had to do it when.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how often did you see these apparently dead people taken to this place?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't wish to lie, but I'm quite certain every other day I had occasion to count them up along the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when you counted them, can you give us an idea of the numbers of people that you saw, apparently dead, lined up along the fence?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: On one particular day, I counted at least five. And on one occasion, I counted 13. There were 13 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were these people just left there or were they taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They left them there. When they took them away, I don't know, but the next day they weren't there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So apparently at some stage when you weren't looking, the bodies were taken away.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear or did someone tell you how they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They were driven off in yellow TAM trucks, the same TAM trucks that brought us our food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the people, the prisoners that were kept in the "white house," and I know you said you couldn't see in it, but did you know of a woman being kept in that "white house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that and I saw her coming out of the "white house" when she went with the men for breakfast or lunch, whatever it was. But once a day I would see her.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe her condition when you saw her?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I didn't see her beaten up. On the contrary. She was a very brave young girl and she would hold her head high when she walked from the "white house" to go to have her meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was she the only woman kept in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why she was kept in the "white house" and not with you women in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, probably she was an extremist compared to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know her name?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Her name was Hajra Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did she survive the camp, so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: She stayed on in the camp after I left. But afterwards nobody ever heard of her, so I have my doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you were in the camp, did you also know of a prisoner there by the name of Nizvet Suljic?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Nizvet Suljic was my neighbour, and I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you able to observe about him?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I saw him twice when he came to breakfast. On one occasion he told me in passing that my apartment had been taken over by somebody. Somebody was living in it; he didn't know who. On another occasion I saw him going back from being interrogated and he was walking in front of a guard. He was wavering; he was going left and right because he had been beaten so he wasn't very stable on his feet. I saw him that same day dead in one of the fork lorries. He was taken across the pista and taken off somewhere. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in the camp on the 12th of July, which was at that time, in that year, a Serb holiday known as Petrov Day?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I was in Omarska on the 12th of July. It is an Orthodox holiday which is celebrated in the traditional manner, and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in particular, can you recall the evening of -- the eve of Petrov Day?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you tell Their Honours what you remember seeing on the eve of Petrov Day when you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I know that they set fire to these tyres instead of torches. I don't know what they used to do when they could celebrate it properly, but I know that these dumper tyres were set fire to on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once they set the fire going, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of light everywhere about. You could smell smoke; it was an unpleasant smell. There was a lot of shouting, cries, shots, that kind of thing. All kinds of things that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it shouting because people were celebrating or was it shouting because people were distressed; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I think they were shouting because they were mistreated, because when you celebrate you usually sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see any of the prisoners following that night or that evening in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly now where the prisoners were, but I know that on that particular morning, when we went off to the restaurant, that I saw a large FAP lorry loaded with dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there more bodies that day than what you'd seen on previous occasions, or was it about the same number?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Not the same number, no. A TAM truck looks different than a large FAP lorry; those are two quite different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The large FAP lorry, was it loaded? Can you give us a better description of what you saw with this large lorry?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I saw a full lorry-load of dead bodies covered with a nylon covering, nylon foil, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, can you recall, when you were in the camp at Omarska, occasions from time to time when busloads of prisoners would arrive?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I remember it well. I remember the buses well and we called them -- referred to them as the black Marica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when they arrived? What can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: When they arrived, all the guards would gather together and beat them. They would shout and cry, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the camp, did you know an inmate, a prisoner there by the name of Nedzad Seric?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Nedzad. Nedzad Seric, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what you saw of him when he was there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: When I came to the camp, I noticed him because he was very thin, emaciated, and he had some signs of beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know what his position was in the community prior to being in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: He was an investigating judge in the Prijedor court. Afterwards he was a lawyer, an attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anything happen to him while you were in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Something did happen but what, I don't know. Anyway, he disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when the women you were sleeping with were in the rooms at night, do you recall anything happening during the night when you were in your sleeping quarters?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're thinking of. Could you explain what you mean, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were any of the women ever called out while you were in your sleeping quarters at night-time?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who called them out?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was pitch black.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to tell us the names, but were they officials at the camp or were they other prisoners or what? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Not the prisoners but the officials. Whether they were the guards or the wardens, I don't really know. But I do know that she was called out on one occasion, she didn't go out, and the inmate next to her said, "Jadranka's in another room." However, the next night Jadranka Cigelj was called out again and taken out this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you see her, Jadranka Cigelj, when she came back into the room after she had been taken out?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Not when she came back, I saw her a day later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: All right. When you saw her a day later, what did you -- can you describe her condition, her emotional state?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. When I saw her a day later, it was just by chance that I happened to be going to the WC, and she was in the bathroom. There was a shower, actually, and her back was turned to me. She didn't notice me at all, but I saw on her right thigh an enormous bruise like this, and on those last -- in those last days, Jadranka Cigelj kept crying all the time. I didn't have the courage to ask her what happened or to ask her where she got that enormous bruise on her right thigh.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when she was crying, did anyone try to comfort her during this time?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: We all comforted her but we didn't know the real reason for her tears because she didn't tell, at least not me, what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the Omarska camp, at any time were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when was that, approximately, when were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but after 15 days of my stay there, I was taken upstairs for interrogation. I was interrogated by Miro Zoric, and there was another man there whom I don't know. He had a short-sleeved shirt on and a dark blue sleeveless vest. He was shortish. That's as much as I can say to describe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they ask you in the interrogation? What questions did they put to you?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: In the course of the interrogation, they wanted me to show them the opening through which one could climb up to my building and how many -- and which men had come to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did you say to them when they asked you these questions?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Of course I couldn't answer those questions, because I am single and no one came to my apartment. Secondly, on my staircase where I lived, there was no passage, there was no opening to reach the attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did the interrogation last for, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Approximately 45 minutes my interrogation lasted, and their attempts to force me to admit that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they threaten you in any way during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They did. No one beat me or touched me, but towards the end of the interrogation, he said to me that they do not have the habit of beating women but that I would be beaten. I answered that I was in their hands, they could do what they wanted with me, but that they should believe me that I really knew nothing at all about those things. At the end, when they let me go, they told me that I would be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were shift commanders and shifts in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you -- from your recollection of what occurred in the Omarska camp, can you tell Their Honours how the shifts worked as best you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: You mean how they worked, how the shifts worked?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell us how long the shifts were, can you remember, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I do. They worked seven hours, they were on duty, and 24 hours they were off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. And were different men on at different times?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were there different shift commanders at different times?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Different commanders, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any variation in the way you were treated from one particular shift to another?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And tell us, what sort of variations could you observe between shifts?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, Krkan's shift was the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Because they were the roughest in their treatment both of us women and the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in terms of the women, what do you say, how were they rough with the women on Krkan's shift?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They called us all kinds of names. They swore at us. They cursed Tito and Alija. That we were ordinary hens. That we were sitting there like idiots. Would we like coffee with cream or without cream, and we should be filmed naked and bathed with hoses and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier actually seeing people hosed out front of the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you tell Their Honours what type of hose they were using to hose these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They would take the prisoners out in groups, and it's a hose I can describe as a thick pipe for fire extinguishing, for extinguishing fires, and it was those hoses that they used to bathe them and make fun of them because the pressure was so strong that people would fall down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the shift commander Krkan that you testified about when you were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I wonder if you would do something, would you mind looking around the courtroom and see if you see the person that you know as Krkan, and if you do, would you please point out to that person for me? Take your time.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Can I get up?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly you can, yes.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The first on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: First on the right facing you?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, facing me. As I look at him, the first on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I think the witness has identified --

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: May I sit down?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we need to get a bit better description, yes. We need for you to actually -- the first on the right is a guard, you see.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The commander. The shift commander, the first man on the right is the shift commander known as Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay. Tell me what is the colour of the coat that that man has on. If you can stand up and have a look again.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I think he's wearing a dark blue jacket or a black one with a grey tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And perhaps you might -- just to make sure, can you go over a bit closer and point with your finger at the person just so that we're 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: How far can I move?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You can take your headset off and point with your finger at the person. Just so there's no doubt about that, just walk over.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: That is Mr. Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think the record might reflect, Your Honour, the witness has identified ... Excuse me, Your Honours, I'm just checking my notes. Just one little question I'd like to ask you and then we will be finished. The -- well, I will be finished at least. The person that interrogated you, I think you said his name was Miroslav Zoric; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know him before you were in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know what position he had prior to being in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I think he was a teacher. I don't know exactly what subject he taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was his duties in the camp, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: This Miro Zoric, you mean? He worked as an interrogator throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. I think we shall have a break now before beginning the cross-examination so the Defence can organise themselves, and so we are having a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take your seat. Mr. Krstan Simic, how are we going to proceed? In what order are you going to cross-examine? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, today, again, we will follow the order of the indictment in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Madam, you are now going to answer questions which the Defence attorneys are going to put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, you may begin. Please take care to ask the witness questions, not to engage in a discussion with the witness and not to make comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hrnic.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I have a few very short questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You said you got there on the 20th. How did you reach Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I arrived in a black Marica, as we call it, the police van.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony you spoke about two rooms used by security personnel.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Was anything written on the doors of those rooms? Did you notice anything written there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Madam Hrnic, there were a lot of people in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you notice or hear of any parcels coming for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I personally can't say much. I know that they arrived; they were distributed to some inmates. Who sent them, I don't know. Most probably relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Who brought them there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Miro Kvocka. Kvotca [phoen] or Kvocka. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: How did he bring them?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: In a Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Hrnic, you said you acquired a pension as a result of your service as a seamstress.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the police ever?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Ms. Hrnic, do you know what work posts exist in the police?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Well, do you know how the police is organised?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I suppose the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the organisation of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Perhaps only when I go there for my identification card.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: So those were your only contacts with the SUP.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: In your company there was an employment system. Do you have any knowledge as to how people were assigned to their work posts in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, excuse me. I don't understand why you are asking this question. The witness mentioned the SUP because the witness went to the SUP before going to the Omarska camp. So I don't understand why you're asking her this question. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness made certain conclusions so we wish to clear up the question of her knowledge of things that she referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but ask questions in the context that the witness spoke in, not in general terms. The witness is not an expert on the organisation of SUP. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I was just going to end there anyway. Thank you very much, Ms. Hrnic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this Defence team has no cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I see now Mr. Fila. The witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hrnic.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have a few short questions for you and please give me short answers so we'll get it over with quickly.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that food was brought in a yellow car; do you know from where?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it true that it wasn't prepared in the facility itself?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it was prepared outside of these buildings shown on the model?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned shifts. You recognised one of the leaders, Krkan. Can you give us the names of some people working in that shift?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I only know the nicknames, not their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then a few nicknames.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They are called -- we called this one "coffee with cream" because he kept teasing us. Later on, I learned that they called him "Pop". Whether that was his nickname or whether his surname was Popovic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Go on then, please.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Then I know someone called Zivko. Please don't insist because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Hrnic, in answer to each of my questions, you can say "I do know" or "I don't know".

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that the guards insulted you?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they do this of their own accord or following orders?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see anyone come and give an order to someone to say such and such a thing?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that, and I don't know whether they did it following orders, but that they insulted me, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you, perhaps, notice certain guards doing it repeatedly, constantly like this one coffee with cream, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: All those guards were insolent. They were all insolent. That's all that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about Krkan's shift, and it was the shift that I named. All of us feared them and if that is enough for you, sir, that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you were: How many guards were there who would insult? I'm interested in the number roughly.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I know that in one shift there would be 15 guards, but all 15 of them did not come to the restaurant at the same time. Sometimes it was one, sometimes another. Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, you can say whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: For instance I know one of the guards called Drazenko who was the worst towards all the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And which shift was he in?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know which shift he was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that the inmates came to eat in three minutes.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Not the guards, the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, just wait for me to complete the question. Can you tell us, because you were staying in the restaurant, when those meals began and how many came in a group and when they ended?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I said that depended on when the meal arrived, when breakfast arrived. From 9.00 a.m. and until 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. They would come this groups of 30 or 31. One would come, the others would go, back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And they all had three minutes each?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, all had three minutes only.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was the time limited to three minutes because otherwise their turn would never come?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned that you did the washing up, with water?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Of course with water.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did the water come from?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: It was -- water was brought in. We had to pour water into these washing basins when the water stopped, when there was no water in the tap.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but when there was tap water, was it the normal sort of water that you used to wash up, and did you drink that water?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it normal water?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It was industrial water.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Water that is not for drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This water in the pipes, where did it -- how did it reach those pipes, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I know that they brought in the water with a reservoirs, truck reservoirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is: When you opened the tap or when you flush in the toilet, was that water brought in tanks, in reservoirs?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you're saying that that water was industrial water?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: What I am saying is that we used industrial water and we drank that water, and that water was brought in tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the water in the tap, was that industrial water, I'm asking you. Please give me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So which water was industrial water according to you?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned Petrovdan as being the 12th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us -- a day before the 12th is the 11th, a day after the 12th is the 13th; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what day the 11th, the 12th or the 13th these tyres were burned, and on what day did you see this larger number of bodies being placed on the truck? Prior to the Petrovdan celebration, the night before, was that the 11th, madam?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Can we put it this way then: On the night between the 11th and 12th, that evening, that night, the tyres were burned that you mentioned and the next day, you saw --

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I saw a full truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, you saw bodies, so it was on Petrovdan in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. The event itself, am I right in saying that you didn't see the event itself, you just heard about; it is that correct, heard this burning of tyres, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I was in the room upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From that room in which you stayed, can you see the "white house" or the pista from there? That night when you were sleeping, of course, that's different.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I understood you. From the room, you could see part of the pista and the "white house".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you then see, where you could see -- the place you could see, that there was nothing there?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't looking. We were -- we kept very small, you know, we had to lie down and we just heard. We weren't allowed to do anything else and I say this, I hope you believe me, but we heard screams, we heard these orgies, we heard these shots. We felt fire. There was light coming from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's all right, madam, there's no need to get excited. I have already heard you say what you said today, so you could see, but you didn't see; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, we weren't allowed to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there somebody in the room who prevented you from looking?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On that particular night like all the other nights, were you alone in your room, you women?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what prevented you from getting up and going to the window and having a look out through the window?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: There was a guard on the roof and we called him the "machine-gunist" because there was a machine-gun set up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's on the roof not in the room; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, actually it's not a roof, it's a flat roof, and they were positioned there. And it was sort of security for the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this machine-gunist prevented you from going to the window and looking out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm telling you once again that I personally did not get up. Perhaps somebody else did but I, myself, did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Madam, in the course of the night, was it possible for you to go outside, was there a guard in front of the room?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: It was possible for us to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether there was a guard posted in front of your room in the corridor in front of your rooms?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: The guards were a little lower down. They had a table there sitting around drinking coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't think they would be sitting around drinking coffee during the night and I'm asking you about night-time.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I did not go out that night so I don't know whether they were there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. It's my fault, I'm not talking about that particular night, I'm talking about generally speaking at night, was there a guard there and where was he sitting?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: If they were sitting, they didn't have to drink coffee all night, there was enough beer to go around for the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Hrnic, I'm asking you at night, from 7.00 at night until 7.00 in the morning, was there a guard or not?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a guard. Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I cannot, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know any of the guards by name, the guards that were on night duty?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I do not know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Was it possible for you to leave your room, to go up to the roof, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I see. No. But someone from your room went down the corridor and went on the roof, did they?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: How could they pass and go up to the roof? They didn't dare. We weren't allowed to. Even if we wanted to, we didn't dare and couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Hrnic, that is what I say, but there was a witness who said that they left your room and got up onto the roof; that's why I'm asking you. But thank you for your answer. Could you please indicate to us, if that is at all possible, you mentioned a fence of some kind, a wire fence, where was that wire fence? Can you show us, please?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just point. You can just point to where it was.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: It was by the "white house," up above the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean towards the Judges? What do you mean "in front," "above"?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: This is the "white house," and when I say -- I mean above the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Looking at it from your angle of vision, how does it lie?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm showing you, sir. It was straight across there. The fence was straight across there. That there is the "red house," and in front of this fencing, the bodies were lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the fence was between the "white" and "red house"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was its direction and position?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: It went in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I see. So the space between the "white house" and the "red house" was cut across by a fence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you mean from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was actually from the hangar, but it was in between those two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know a lady called (redacted)

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was she in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was, in another room.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do you know about her behaviour?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about her behaviour, but I know that she would usually distribute the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did she have any cooperation with the management of the camp, and would she give out information about the inmates?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't hear that. But I know that she was very frequently with Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. But you don't happen to know whether she would report somebody or whether they thought that she might be reporting people?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that. I didn't hear anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be all. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Tosic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence counsel shall not be cross-examining this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tosic. Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness either, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovan Simic. Mr. Niemann, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Hrnic. I hope I've pronounced your name properly.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've done it well. Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just a few clarifications to ask you about. You mentioned that you would see bodies at the fence; one day it was five bodies, one day it was 15 bodies. Then they were taken away the next day, they were not there, that they were taken away later in a yellow TAM truck. Did you ever know how these dead bodies were killed? Because you said that they were dead.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Can I put something right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Make a correction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I didn't say there were 15 of them, because I counted 13 at the most on one particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. But they were dead?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, yes, dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But how were they killed, you have no idea?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then you spoke about the eve of Petrovdan in Omarska when you heard shouts, tyres burning, and shots, and you saw in the morning a large lorry with dead bodies. What was this occasion? Was it a religious day? Was it a national festivity? Why were there an exceptional number of killed people; do you know? Was there a fight?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I know that it is an Orthodox holiday and it's called Petrovdan, St. Peter's day, and I said that a moment ago. I didn't understand -- did you ask me if there was a fight of any kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Why were there so many people killed that night or that day? Was there some kind of insurrection in the camp of the inmates, for instance, or was it just an opportunity to execute?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I think there might have been an uprising of some -- I doubt that there was an uprising. But why they killed so many people, I don't know. They were killed, they were loaded up on the truck, they were covered with this nylon foil, that is true, and I don't know what else I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, in the event there was an uprising, the inmates, did they have any kind of weapons, or were their weapons completely taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No. The detainees were bare-handed, just like I am now. All I have is my glasses in front of me. That's how they were, bare-handed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke about several people who seemed to be important people and who were either badly treated or disappeared. You spoke about a judge Seric who disappeared, about a professor of mathematics, Crnkic, and about Dr. Begic. Were these people eminent people? Were they chosen particularly to be mistreated or to disappear?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They were all highly distinguished people. A doctor can never be an ordinary man, nor can a professor. They are intellectuals. In a word, intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They had some kind of priority in the bad treatment or in disappearing?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, in my opinion, that need not be so. But intellectuals and rich people, they suffered most, and of course the ordinary people as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Why did they arrest you in particular? And then they threatened you, as you mentioned, in the interrogation, they threatened to execute you. Is there something in particular which they suspected?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They had no reason to suspect me of anything because, first and foremost, I never meddled in politics at all. From day one I was an orphan and my prime goal was to survive, and for 33 years I was an ordinary worker, a seamstress. I had to reach my norms to make a living for myself. So the only reason was that I was a Muslim and they wanted to take away what little property I had so that I couldn't return anywhere and leave Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said you had 17 other ladies with you in the same room, Hasiba, Avdija, Valida, and so on. Was there any reason for their arrest? Were they some kind of, as you said -- you spoke about another woman, Hajra Hodzic, who was more or less an outspoken, perhaps, fighter. The others too, did they represent any opposition? Why were they, in particular, taken? Did they take any woman haphazardly?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you don't -- yes?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Every one of those women will come here, and then they can state their reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. You don't know much about them?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you only knew about Jadranka who was called out at night.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I know Jadranka as a -- well, she's a girl compared to me because I'm much older than her, and I knew her when I came to the camp, and a few other women as well, I knew them. But I knew nothing about her. It was only in the camp that I learnt that she was -- that she had studied law and that she was in the room with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were the other women called out at night, apart from Jadranka?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Not at night, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: During the day?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: During the day one young girl was taken out, but I don't know for what reason. Whether it was by force or whether for any other reasons, adultery, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you felt when Jadranka came back that there was a reason.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I didn't think there was a reason. I just -- well, I don't know how to answer that question of yours. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I don't want to put you in any difficulty. You said that she was crying all the time and that she had enormous bruises.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But there was no other information?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Nothing more, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you said that Kvocka brought parcels. Was it for all the inmates or was it for special people?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Only for special people, not for everybody, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
