utterances.text: Who were these special people; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, I could enumerate them. There was Dedo Crnalic and his wife's uncle or uncle's son, I'm not quite sure; then Ziko Crnalic; then he brought it for Braco Burazerovic and for some other people as well, but unfortunately those people are no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Last question. You said that Krkan's shift was the roughest. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In what way was it the roughest?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I have already said that they beat the detainees most on their way to meals and coming back from meals, and that they mistreated us women; that is to say, they abused us verbally. They didn't beat us but said all manner of things to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mean the other shifts did not beat the inmates, only this shift used to beat the inmates?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of them beat the inmates but these were the roughest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much, Ms. Hrnic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Hrnic, you said that the food was brought in from the outside, and I think you said that it was brought in in the same kind of yellow TAM trucks that were used to remove the bodies when they were piled up near the "white house." Did you have any opportunity to see what kind of people were either driving those trucks or brought the food into the kitchen from those trucks? In other words, were they soldiers, police, civilians? Did you ever see what kind of people were bringing the food in?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I did see the people, yes. I don't know their names. They were not wearing uniforms. They were wearing their work clothes because they were workers of the iron ore mine of Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Those yellow TAM trucks that they brought the food in or that carried away the bodies, did those have the labels of the mining company on them, or they were just yellow trucks?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: They were just yellow trucks. The traditional, I apologise, I can't seem to say the word, but they were vehicles belonging to the mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. On the food, one other question. You said that most of the time it was bread and either some kind of sour beans or a weak cabbage soup. Did anything have to be done in the kitchen of the restaurant or did it come in buckets and went straight to be distributed to the inmates?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I have already said that the food was brought in ready-prepared. Now, where it was brought in from, I don't know. I heard that it was from the separation department. But the food was not cooked in the restaurant, it was just distributed, and the dishes were washed. So the food would come in ready-prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Another question. On the day of Petrovdan, on the evening whichever evening it was you heard the sounds of the -- and smelled the tyres being burned when you were in your -- and heard the noises when you were in your sleeping rooms, do you have any knowledge of what shift was on that evening, which commander's shift was on duty that evening?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is: During any time, no matter whose shift it was, whether it was Krkan's shift or some other shift, when the women were called names or were verbally harassed by the guards, did you, on any of those occasions, ever see the shift commander there when that happened no matter who he was? In other words, did the guards do this when their commander, their shift commander or any camp official was not around or did you see any occasion when there was a camp official or a shift commander around and the guards still verbally harassed the women?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. Please believe me when I say that I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I believe you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hrnic, I have just one question for you. You gave us the impression that the commander of the camp was Zeljko Meakic and that after that, Kvocka came, and after Kvocka, after Kvocka left, that Prcac came. What did you observe? What did you see or did anybody tell you that? How did you learn that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, this was the impression I gained. I gained the impression that they were the wardens, because the leaders had to talk to them, to consult them. In a word, well, they all would say Zeljko and Kvocka are the wardens. All of them said that. Everybody said that. I didn't ask them whether they were the wardens or whether somebody else was the warden, but I viewed them too as being wardens. If I was wrong, well, I don't know. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On occasion, either Zeljko Meakic or perhaps Miroslav Kvocka, did they introduce themselves as being the commanders of the camp or deputy commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Not to me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to others, do you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, Madam Hrnic, if you were to look around this room and the way in which you have observed the functioning of this courtroom, who is the coordinator of the courtroom? Who orchestrates things? Or let me put the question to you differently: Who is the commander in this room?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, I would assume that it is you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm asking for your opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, it is you, sir. And among others, your two colleagues working with you, and I think the main -- my main questioner is the gentleman, that's how I see things. Whether that is indeed so, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, why have you arrived at that conclusion, can you explain that to us? How did you bring in that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: First of all you are sitting in the position you are sitting in. You seem to be the main person, the responsible person, the number one person, in my opinion. Then to your left and right, those are your -- the people that you confer with. That's it. That's my vision of things. If I'm wrong, please put me right. I don't know, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are a very wise lady and you have a lot of experience so it is always possible based on observations to make conclusions who is the man in charge, who the responsible people are, and who the people who are not responsible. I can conclude that, Ms. Hrnic; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure in the sense you were speaking of. Were you referring to the camp and who was responsible in the camp or what, or do you mean here in this courtroom? What were you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both.

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, in the camp, the responsible person was the commander. It was them, they were the most responsible. Then, there were their deputies and they were -- well not the guards, but the brigadiers, shall I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, madam. So on the basis of one's observation, is it possible to draw certain conclusions as to who is the number one man or not?

utterances.speaker: ZUHRA HRNIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, you must be able to conclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Madam Hrnic. I don't think we have any exhibits to tender. You have completed your testimony here. You have answered questions put to you by Mr. Niemann and the questions put to you by the Defence counsel and, indeed, by the Judges. Is there anything that you would like to say at this point which hasn't been asked of you yet and you would like to state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. We should like to take this opportunity to extend our gratitude to you once again and wish you bon voyage to your place of residence and your country of residence and you are now going to leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you one and all. You are very proper in your conduct towards me, and wishing me bon voyage back to my own country, that would be my greatest wish, but I do doubt that I can go back there. But that is the only wish I have, to go back to my apartment and my town. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't want to interrupt when Your Honours were asking questions, but when Judge Riad was asking a question, there seemed to be a question whether or not there was an uprising, not confusion on Your Honours' part, but confusion, I think, in the translation. As I heard the translation it was, "There was no uprising," or words to that effect. But it did come across at one stage as if the witness was saying there was an uprising, and I thought I, perhaps, should clarify that matter, Your Honours. I think the translation clearly was there was no uprising, if I may assist, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Niemann, I was in this confusion too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis or Mr. Niemann, I don't know. I see Mr. Simic, Ms. Hollis. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether Ms. Hollis is going to raise the same issue, but we had certain contacts during the break regarding the status of the witness that is about to come. We fear that we will not be able to complete the cross-examination. The next hearing will be in 14 days, and keeping the witness under the obligation not to have any contacts, we were discussing the possibility of not starting the examination-in-chief today, but rather that we have the Status Conference now. So I'm speaking on behalf of the entire Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. There is an order and I have -- I think you have deprived Ms. Hollis of a good opportunity to say this. It is up to her to propose this -- to raise this matter, but your task has been facilitated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It certainly has, Your Honour, and we thank the Defence for doing that. We did have this discussion about the witness. We are in Your Honours' hands. We believe it is possible that cross-examination would not be completed today so we simply wanted to put the matter to Your Honours to determine how you wanted to proceed. We can either proceed and do as much as we can today or we could begin afresh with this witness at the beginning of the next session. So again, we simply raise the matter for Your Honours' determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: How long do you propose the direct will be?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour we believe the direct will be between one and one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Ms. Hollis, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the Defence, do you have any idea how much time you will need for the cross-examination? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no idea until we hear the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But Ms. Hollis said one hour to one and a half hours, the duration. Of course the problem is the content. We are concerned, because it always means that a witness will have to come and go back, and come back again. If we thought that we could begin and finish today, it would be better because the witness would not have to come back again. But I fear that working under pressure and forcing the Defence counsel to proceed quickly is something I would rather not do. I think that the Chamber should discipline the debate but should not prevent a debate. So I think there is a risk of juxtaposing many considerations, and perhaps we could go on working until 6.00, because we have a Status Conference too and that is a great risk for the proper rendering of justice. It is in the interests of justice not to begin; however, in the interests of the administration of justice, it is to begin. However, as justice considerations are more important, I think that we should have a break and begin with the Status Conference. I think that would be the best solution. We're going to have a half-hour break, and after that, immediately we'll proceed with the Status Conference. It will be a public hearing. Because there was some hesitation before and I think the parties prefer us all to be in robes, so that is how we're going to work for the Status Conference, in public and in robes. A half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 12.15 p.m., to be followed by a Status Conference
